bp: Many web systems must describe the same object from several sources at once. A video can have images, text, audio, user comments, and behavior logs; a product can have photos, seller text, category clues, and click history. The task is not just to choose one label, because one object may belong to many labels at the same time. The paper studies this multi-source, many-label setting under two pressures that ordinary deployments create. First, some sources are often missing: a page may have text but no image, or an item may have behavior logs but no clean description. Second, new labels keep appearing as the web changes. A model that only understands the old label set becomes stale. E2PL is meant for this combined situation: keep learning new classes while still making predictions when arbitrary views are absent, without letting the number of learned settings explode.
wh: The hard part is that missing sources and new labels multiply each other's difficulty. If every item always arrived with the same views, the model could learn a stable recipe for combining them. If the label set never changed, it could tune itself around one fixed vocabulary of possible answers. Real web data violates both comforts. Different examples can lose different views, so the system must know how to act when image is missing, when text is missing, when both are present, or when several other combinations occur. At the same time, class-incremental learning asks the model to add new labels without discarding its old competence. A direct missing-view design can create separate settings for every subset of views, but the number of subsets doubles whenever another view is added. That is the exponential parameter growth the abstract names, and it makes web-scale use impractical.
naive: A smart beginner might train one classifier for the complete data and then patch missing cases with simple fixes: fill absent views with zeros, ignore the missing source, or train a separate small model for each pattern of available views. The first two fixes blur together very different situations. A zero image is not the same as no image, and ignoring a source can hide which evidence is trustworthy. The separate-model idea respects the missing pattern, but it breaks as soon as there are many views, because every combination needs its own learned parameters. The beginner might also retrain whenever new classes appear, but that is expensive and can overwrite what the system already learned about old labels.
ap: E2PL's central move is to guide a shared model with small learned instructions rather than build a new full model for every situation. A prompt here means a compact learned piece of input-side guidance that tells the model what kind of task or missing-view condition it is facing. The paper uses task-tailored prompts for the arrival of new classes and missing-aware prompts for whichever views are absent. The important efficiency move is prototype tensorization. Instead of storing a separate missing-aware prompt for every possible subset of views, E2PL represents those prompts from smaller atomic parts and combines the parts. Atomic tensor decomposition is the mathematical language for this: it describes a large table of combinations through a limited set of reusable factors, reducing parameter growth from exponential in the number of views to linear.
mech: The input is a multi-view, multi-label example: several possible sources describe one web object, some of those sources may be unavailable, and the correct answer may include several labels. The learning setting also unfolds over time, because new classes are introduced after earlier classes have already been learned. E2PL first separates the guidance problem into two kinds of prompts. Task-tailored prompts tell the model how to adapt to the current class-incremental task, so the system can attach new label knowledge without treating the whole problem as frozen. Missing-aware prompts tell the model what evidence pattern it is seeing, so an item with only text is not handled the same way as an item with text plus image. The expensive version would prepare a distinct prompt for every missing-view pattern. E2PL instead builds those prompts through prototype tensorization: each view contributes compact atomic pieces, and a prompt for a particular missing pattern is assembled from the relevant pieces. The dynamic contrastive learning strategy then compares different missing-view patterns so the model learns their dependencies, meaning it is pushed to keep related cases close in behavior while still respecting their differences. The output is a multi-label prediction over the current class set, with fewer learned prompt parameters than the exhaustive missing-pattern design would require.
math: The main mathematical idea is factorization: describe a large set of possible combinations using smaller reusable parts. If there are many views, the list of present-or-missing patterns grows like a branching tree; each added view doubles the number of possible patterns. A full table with one prompt per pattern wastes memory because many patterns share structure. Atomic tensor decomposition treats that table as something built from atoms. In everyday terms, it is like describing many outfits by shirts, pants, and shoes instead of listing every complete outfit separately. The paper uses this to turn missing-view prompt parameters from exponential growth into linear growth with respect to the number of views. A second idea is comparison-based learning, called contrastive learning in the abstract: the model is trained by comparing cases or patterns so that related forms of evidence agree more than unrelated ones. Here the comparison is dynamic because missing patterns differ across examples and tasks. The underlying tradeoff is compression versus detail. Tensorization saves parameters by sharing parts, but the shared parts must still preserve the meaningful differences between missing-view situations. The class-incremental side adds the stability-versus-adaptation tradeoff: learn new labels while keeping old label behavior useful.
dots: This paper sits at the intersection of several recurring conference problems. It is about multi-view learning because the object is described by several sources whose evidence must be combined. It is about multi-label classification because the answer is a set of labels rather than a single winner. It is about incremental learning because the label universe expands over time, a pressure also visible in repo entries on graph incremental learning and continual named entity recognition, where new classes arrive without permission to forget old ones. It is also an efficiency paper, because the key obstacle is not only prediction quality but the cost of representing every missing-view pattern separately. The connection to similarity and comparison appears in the dynamic contrastive part: different incomplete versions of the same broader situation must teach the model what should remain consistent. The connection to compression appears in tensor decomposition, which keeps the reusable structure and avoids storing every combination by hand.
ww: The approach should improve over the naive design because it matches the shape of the problem. Missing views are not random labels that require unrelated models; they are combinations of the same underlying sources. If a system has learned how the text view behaves and how the image view behaves, it should reuse that knowledge when only one is missing or when both are present. Prototype tensorization gives the model a way to reuse those view-level parts instead of memorizing every subset separately. Task-tailored prompts help with the other pressure: new classes can be introduced through compact task guidance rather than rebuilding the whole classifier from scratch each time. The dynamic comparison step helps because missing patterns are related but not identical. It asks the model to notice that two incomplete versions may still refer to the same object-level meaning, while also learning when a missing source removes important evidence. This is why the method can plausibly be both effective and efficient: it shares structure where the world really shares structure.
po: The payoff is a model for the paper's newly formalized task, incomplete multi-view multi-label class incremental learning. According to the abstract, E2PL handles heterogeneous missing views and expanding classes together, while avoiding the parameter explosion that makes exhaustive missing-pattern prompts hard to scale. The concrete efficiency claim is that prototype tensorization reduces prompt parameter complexity from exponential to linear with respect to the number of views. The abstract also reports experiments on three benchmarks where E2PL outperforms prior methods in both effectiveness and efficiency. For web applications, that means a practical route to updating label vocabularies while still using messy, partially observed multi-source data.
limits: The claims depend on the missing-view structure being shareable through atomic parts. If some missing patterns require entirely different reasoning, the compressed tensor representation may hide too much detail. The approach also assumes prompts can carry enough task and missingness information without full retraining. The abstract does not specify the three benchmarks, the kinds of views, the degree of missingness, or how new classes are scheduled, so the deployment boundary is unclear from this evidence alone. It reports better effectiveness and efficiency, but the abstract does not prove behavior under adversarial missingness, highly rare labels, noisy views, or settings where old and new classes conflict strongly.
